title: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS JESUS? THE BIBLICAL ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS JESUS? THE BIBLICAL ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.

When the child you raised to love God walks away from everything you taught them, should you close the door to protect your faith—or leave it open because Jesus never stopped loving the lost? What Scripture actually teaches about rebellion, boundaries, repentance, parental heartbreak, and the kind of grace that refuses to surrender the truth.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that only a Christian parent understands.
It is hearing your grown child say, “I don't believe in God anymore.”
And suddenly, the room feels different.
This is the same child whose tiny hands you once folded together in prayer.
The same child you carried into church before they could walk.
The same child you taught to say, “Jesus loves me,” before they understood what those words meant.
You remember their first Bible.
Their first Sunday school lesson.
Maybe even the day they were baptized.
And now?
They tell you Christianity is not for them.
They question the Bible you taught them to trust. They reject the Savior you have spent your life following. Perhaps they mock the faith that carried you through your darkest nights.
And somewhere between your disappointment and your fear, a terrible question begins forming.
Should I cut my own child out of my life because they have rejected Jesus?
Before you answer, I want you to picture something.
A father standing outside his house.
Looking down a road.
Waiting for someone who has broken his heart.
Someone who has dishonored his family.
Someone who has taken what was given to him and wasted it.
The father has every reason to be angry.
Every reason to close the door.
Every reason to say, “You made your choice. Now live with it.”
But when he finally sees his son approaching in the distance, something happens that changes the entire story.
He runs.
And if you are a Christian parent wrestling with whether to cut off your adult child, you need to understand why Jesus told that story.
Because the answer is deeper than simply saying, “Always welcome them,” or “Cut them off until they repent.”
And getting it wrong can wound a family for generations.
Jesus tells us in Luke 15:11–32 about a younger son who demands his inheritance before his father dies.
In that culture, the request was deeply insulting. The son wanted the benefits of his father's possessions without remaining under his father's household.
He wanted the inheritance.
But not the relationship as it had been.
He wanted freedom.
But not the responsibility that came with it.
So the father divided his property.
And the son left.
Notice what the father did not do.
He did not chase his son into the distant country and force him to return.
He did not pretend the son's decisions were wise.
He did not finance an endless rebellion.
But neither does Jesus describe the father declaring that his son was permanently dead to him and forbidden ever to return.
The son eventually squandered everything.
He became desperate.
Hungry.
Humiliated.
And in his misery, he remembered his father's house.
Luke 15:17 says, in the King James Version, “And when he came to himself.”
The Greek expression is εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν (eis heauton de elthōn).
Literally, the wording conveys the idea of coming to himself.
It is a powerful picture of a man beginning to recognize the reality of his condition.

But we must be careful here. The expression does not mean every struggling or unbelieving adult child is irrational, mentally unwell, or incapable of thoughtful disagreement. Jesus is describing this particular son's awakening within the parable.
And then comes the moment that should stop every wounded parent in their tracks.
Luke 15:20 says:
“But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
The Greek word translated “had compassion” is ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (esplanchnisthē), from a verb describing deep, inward compassion.
Not reluctant tolerance.
Not cold permission to enter the house.
Compassion.
The father saw his son before the son reached him.
And he ran.
But do not miss something equally important.
The son returned acknowledging his sin.
The father did not need to call evil good in order to welcome his child home.
Grace did not erase the truth.
And truth did not extinguish grace.
That is the tension Christian parents must learn to carry.
Because some parents believe loving their child means approving every decision that child makes.
Others believe standing for biblical truth requires withdrawing affection until the child changes.
Scripture gives us a more demanding way.
A way that requires conviction without cruelty.
Love without compromise.
Boundaries without revenge.
And faithfulness without pretending we control another person's soul.
Consider this carefully.
Your adult child may reject Christianity.
But does that mean you must reject your child?
No. Scripture does not establish a universal command requiring Christian parents to sever relationships with adult children simply because those children no longer profess faith in Christ.
That distinction matters enormously.
In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul addresses a serious case of public, unrepentant sexual immorality within the Corinthian church.
He instructs the congregation to exercise discipline toward someone who claims membership among believers while persisting in such conduct.
But in verses 9–13, Paul explicitly distinguishes those inside the church from those outside it.
In 1 Corinthians 5:12, he asks:
“For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?”
The context concerns church discipline, not a blanket rule for parents to abandon unbelieving relatives.
A professing Christian living in open, serious, unrepentant sin presents a different pastoral question from an adult child who openly says they are no longer a believer.
Even then, the nature of the relationship matters.
Church membership is not identical to parenthood.
And the authority of a local congregation is not the same as a parent's authority over an independent adult.
We must never turn a passage about church discipline into a weapon Scripture itself has not authorized.
Some will point to Matthew 10:34–37, where Jesus warns that allegiance to Him may divide even the closest families.
And yes, those words are serious.
Christ must come first.
A parent must never deny Jesus to preserve a relationship.
But putting Christ first does not automatically mean refusing to speak to an unbelieving son or daughter.
Jesus warns that following Him may bring division. He does not command parents to manufacture that division whenever a child disagrees with their faith.
There is a difference between suffering rejection because you follow Christ and deliberately rejecting someone to prove that you follow Christ.
Please read that again.
There is a difference between suffering rejection because you follow Christ and deliberately rejecting someone to prove that you follow Christ.
And if that sentence makes you uncomfortable, perhaps it is worth sitting with that discomfort before making a decision that cannot easily be undone.
Because your child is not your enemy.
Ephesians 6:12 reminds believers that our struggle is not ultimately against flesh and blood.
That does not mean your child's decisions have no consequences.
It means your child is not the ultimate enemy to be defeated.
You can disagree with their beliefs.
You can refuse to participate in conduct that violates your conscience.
You can maintain your Christian convictions.
And you can still say:
“You are my child. I love you. I cannot agree with everything you believe or do, but my love for you is not something you have to earn by pretending to believe what I believe.”
Imagine what that kind of sentence might mean to someone who expects nothing but rejection.
Not because it guarantees they will return to Christianity.
It does not.
But because love that is not used as leverage can make honest conversation possible.
And honest conversation matters.
Perhaps your adult child did not walk away because they wanted to live recklessly.
Perhaps they encountered questions they did not know how to answer.
Perhaps they witnessed hypocrisy among Christians.
Perhaps they were hurt by someone who used the Bible to control or shame them.
Perhaps they struggled with suffering, unanswered prayer, or difficult passages of Scripture.
Or perhaps, after serious reflection, they genuinely no longer believe Christianity is true.
You may disagree with their conclusions.
You may believe they are profoundly mistaken.
But if you refuse to listen, how will you understand what they are actually rejecting?
A parent who listens is not necessarily compromising.
Sometimes listening is the beginning of speaking truth wisely.
James 1:19 says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
The Greek phrase ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι (tachys eis to akousai) means “quick to hear.”
Notice that Scripture does not say, “Be quick to win every argument.”
It calls us to hear.
And hearing requires more than waiting for your turn to correct someone.
Some parents have spent years preparing answers to questions their children never actually asked.
Meanwhile, their children have been carrying wounds nobody noticed.
What if, instead of beginning another argument, you asked:
“Can you help me understand what changed?”
“What has your experience of Christianity been like?”
“Did something happen that made trusting God difficult?”
“Have I ever made you feel that you could not be honest with me?”
That last question may be the hardest.
Because it opens the possibility that a parent who sincerely loved Jesus may still have made mistakes.
And Christian parents are not exempt from repentance.
Ephesians 6:4 warns fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
The Greek verb παροργίζετε (parorgizete) refers to provoking or exasperating.
Paul's instruction does not mean parents must avoid every disagreement or difficult correction.
It does mean that the manner in which parents exercise authority matters to God.
A parent can teach true doctrine in a harsh way.
A parent can defend biblical morality while speaking with contempt.
A parent can insist on outward religious behavior while neglecting the child's inner life.
And a parent can be right about an important biblical principle while being wrong in the way they treat another human being.
If that has happened, repentance is not surrendering your faith.
It is practicing it.
You can say:
“I still believe Jesus Christ is Lord. I still believe the gospel is true. But I recognize that I have sometimes spoken to you with anger instead of patience. I am sorry. Will you forgive me?”
There is no contradiction between confessing Christ and confessing your own failures.
In fact, the gospel gives us a reason to do both.
But what about boundaries?
What if your adult child mocks Jesus in your home?
What if they become verbally abusive?
What if they steal from you, threaten your safety, manipulate you financially, or repeatedly violate reasonable household expectations?
Must you tolerate all of that to prove Christian love?
Absolutely not.
Christian love is not permission for abuse.
Forgiveness is not the same as unrestricted access.
Reconciliation is not the same as the immediate restoration of trust.
And a relationship does not become healthy merely because two people share DNA.
Proverbs 22:3 describes the prudent person as one who foresees danger and takes refuge.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
Notice the realism of that verse.
If it be possible.
As much as lieth in you.
Peace requires more than one person's willingness.
You can be responsible for your conduct without being able to control another person's response.
If an adult child is abusive, threatening, or dangerous, a parent may need distance, firm restrictions, professional support, or even complete separation for safety.
That is not the same as cutting someone off merely because they no longer believe in Jesus.
A parent can refuse to fund destructive behavior.
A parent can establish conditions for living in their home.
A parent can end conversations that become abusive.
A parent can say, “I will speak with you when we can treat each other respectfully.”
And in genuinely dangerous situations, a parent can prioritize safety without waiting for the other person to agree.
Love does not require remaining available for harm.
But boundaries should serve truth, safety, and responsibility—not become disguised punishments for unbelief.
That is a crucial difference.
“I cannot allow you to threaten me” is a boundary.
“I will never speak to you again unless you become a Christian” makes affection conditional on religious profession.
Those are not the same thing.
And we should never confuse them.
There is another passage many parents need to hear.
Colossians 4:5–6 instructs believers to walk wisely toward outsiders and let their speech be gracious, seasoned with salt.
The Greek expression ἐν χάριτι (en chariti) means “with grace” or “in grace.”
Paul does not tell Christians to abandon conviction.
He tells them to communicate with grace and wisdom.
If we are called to speak graciously to outsiders, why would we assume that our unbelieving adult children should receive less gracious speech simply because their unbelief hurts us personally?
The pain is real.
But pain does not give us permission to become cruel.
And perhaps this is where the deepest issue begins to surface.
Some Christian parents are not only grieving their child's unbelief.
They are grieving the future they imagined.
The family praying together.
The grandchildren raised in church.
The shared worship.
The familiar traditions.
The certainty that the next generation would carry the same faith.
And when that future begins to disappear, fear can masquerade as righteous anger.
We may say, “I am defending God.”
But underneath, we may also be saying, “I am terrified of losing my child.”
If that is you, God already knows.
You do not have to disguise grief as certainty.
You can bring it to Him.
You can weep.
You can pray.
You can ask for wisdom.
You can admit that you are afraid.
But do not let fear convince you that you must become the Holy Spirit in your child's life.
You cannot manufacture saving faith.
You cannot argue someone into regeneration.
You cannot threaten someone into genuine repentance.
Jesus says in John 6:44:
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.”

That statement comes within Jesus' teaching about the Father's work in bringing people to the Son. Christians have long discussed aspects of its theological implications, but the passage clearly directs attention to God's initiative rather than human coercion.
And Romans 10:17 reminds us that faith comes through hearing the message of Christ.
That is why we bear witness.
Why we teach.
Why we pray.
Why we speak the truth.
But we are not sovereign over the result.
Your calling is faithfulness.
Not control.
You are a parent.
You are not the Savior.
And that truth can be painful before it becomes freeing.
Because you may have to surrender something you never realized you were holding so tightly.
The belief that if you prayed enough, taught enough, disciplined enough, or modeled Christianity well enough, your child would certainly become a lifelong believer.

Proverbs 22:6 speaks of training a child in the way he should go, but this wisdom proverb should not be turned into an unconditional guarantee that every faithfully raised child will profess saving faith as an adult.
The Bible itself shows us that people make real moral and spiritual choices.
Parents bear responsibility for their own faithfulness.
But adult children bear responsibility for their own responses to God.
Your child's unbelief is not, by itself, proof that you failed as a parent.
Nor does your sincerity as a parent prove you made no mistakes.
Both truths can stand together.
And perhaps that is where humility begins.
Now consider Jesus Himself.
John 1:11 says:
“He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
The Son of God knows rejection.
He knows what it means to extend truth and mercy and still be refused.
In Matthew 23:37, Jesus laments over Jerusalem, expressing His desire to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, while confronting their unwillingness.
There is tenderness in that lament.
There is also judgment and seriousness.
Jesus does not pretend rejection is harmless.
But His grief is not cold.
His heart is not indifferent.
And at the cross, the gospel reveals something even greater.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek word συνίστησιν (synistēsin) conveys God's demonstration or commendation of His love.
God's love was demonstrated while we were still sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had earned His attention.
Not after we had become spiritually impressive.
Christ died for the ungodly.
And that is the center of Christianity.
Not parental control.
Not religious appearances.
Not the preservation of a perfect-looking family.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen, offering forgiveness and reconciliation with God to sinners who cannot save themselves.
This does not mean every person is automatically reconciled to God regardless of faith or repentance.
Scripture calls people to repent and believe the gospel.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus saying:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek words μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε (metanoeite kai pisteuete) express the call to repent and believe.
Grace is not permission to remain indifferent to sin.
It is God's undeserved favor revealed supremely in Christ, who calls sinners to turn to Him.
And because salvation is so serious, we must not reduce it to outward compliance.
An adult child who attends church merely to keep parental affection has not necessarily embraced Jesus.
An adult child who says a prayer to stop a family argument has not necessarily experienced genuine conversion.
A child who hides doubts out of fear may look obedient while becoming increasingly isolated.
Would you rather have a child who pretends to believe in order to keep you happy?
Or a child who knows they can speak honestly with you, even when the truth breaks your heart?
Honesty does not guarantee salvation.
But forced religious performance is not the same as saving faith.
And Christian parents should desire genuine faith, not merely the appearance of it.
There is something else we must remember about the father in Luke 15.
He did not run into the distant country and declare the son's rebellion righteous.
He did not rewrite morality to make the relationship comfortable.
But when the son returned, the father did not stand on the porch rehearsing every failure.
He received him with compassion.
He called for a robe.
A ring.
Sandals.
A celebration.
And the father said in Luke 15:24:
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
The Greek word ἀπολωλώς (apolōlōs) means “lost,” and εὑρέθη (heurethē) means “was found.”
The language belongs to the great movement of Luke 15, where Jesus responds to criticism that He welcomes sinners and eats with them.
The lost sheep.
The lost coin.
The lost son.
And the joy associated with finding what was lost.
The parable is ultimately revealing God's mercy toward repentant sinners and confronting the resentment of those who object to that mercy.
It is not a step-by-step parenting manual.
We should not force every detail into a rule about adult children.
But its picture of mercy, repentance, and welcome should deeply shape how Christians understand the heart of God.
And there is another person in the story.
The older brother.
He stayed home.
He obeyed.
He worked.
And when his younger brother returned, he was furious.
He could not understand why someone who had behaved so badly should be received so generously.
Sometimes, Christian parents can begin to resemble that older brother.
We become so focused on the offense that we lose sight of the person.
So determined to uphold righteousness that we begin to resent mercy.
So concerned with what others will think that we forget what grace looks like.
But the father goes out to the older son, too.
He appeals to him.
He does not treat resentment as righteousness.
And the story ends without telling us whether the older brother entered the celebration.
That unfinished ending leaves a question hanging over the listener.
Will you rejoice in mercy?
Or will you remain outside, convinced that someone else's failure has made them unworthy of love?
Perhaps today, that question is not only for your adult child.
Perhaps it is for you.
Because your son or daughter may need to repent of unbelief or sin.
But you may also need to repent of bitterness.
Of pride.
Of contempt.
Of using silence as punishment.
Of caring more about your family's reputation than your child's soul.
Of turning conversations into interrogations.
Of making every birthday, holiday, or family gathering another opportunity for confrontation.
Of confusing the desire to be right with the calling to love.
And before anyone misunderstands me, let me say this clearly.
You should not compromise the gospel to keep peace.
You should not deny Christ.
You should not celebrate what Scripture identifies as sin merely to avoid disagreement.
You should not abandon wise boundaries.
But you also should not make rejection your first response when Christ has called you to love your neighbor, bear witness with gentleness, and entrust judgment to God.
First Peter 3:15 tells believers to be ready to give an answer for their hope, with meekness and fear—that is, gentleness and reverence.
The Greek word πραΰτητος (prautētos) points to gentleness.
Gentleness is not weakness.
It is strength governed by humility.
And sometimes the strongest thing a Christian parent can do is sit across from a grown child, hear something heartbreaking, and refuse to retaliate.
To say:

“I don't agree with you. My faith in Jesus has not changed. But I still want to understand you. I still want to be part of your life where we can have a healthy relationship. And I will never stop praying for you.”
Not as a rehearsed tactic.
Not as emotional pressure.
Not as a promise that everything will turn out the way you want.
But as a sincere expression of love.
Because there may come a day when your child faces a crisis.
A marriage collapses.
A job disappears.
A friendship betrays them.
A grief arrives that no argument can explain away.
And when that day comes, you do not want their first thought to be:
“I cannot call my parents. They only love the version of me that agrees with them.”
You want them to know that you will tell them the truth, but you will not delight in their pain.
That you will not exploit their suffering to win a theological argument.
That they can come to you without being humiliated.
Not because you can guarantee they will return to Jesus.
But because you are determined not to let your own conduct become an unnecessary obstacle to hearing about Him.
And if you are the adult child reading this, perhaps you have been on the other side of that closed door.
Perhaps you told your parents you no longer believed.
And instead of a conversation, you received an ultimatum.
Perhaps they stopped calling.
Perhaps family gatherings became painful.
Perhaps you have spent years wondering whether your parents love you or only the faith they hoped you would share.
I cannot know everything that happened in your family.
And I will not pretend every disagreement is abuse or every parent who sets boundaries is unloving.
But I can tell you this.
Your questions deserve to be heard respectfully.
Your dignity does not disappear because your beliefs have changed.
And whatever human beings have done in the name of Christianity, their failures should not be mistaken for a complete picture of Jesus Christ.
If you are willing, read the Gospels for yourself.
Look at how Jesus treated the proud.
The broken.
The doubting.
The outcast.
The religious hypocrite.
The sinner who knew he needed mercy.
Do not merely examine what people have said about Him.
Examine Him.
And if you have rejected a distorted picture of Christianity, be willing to consider whether the real Jesus is different from the one you were shown.
He does not call you to pretend.
He calls you to truth.
And the gospel announces that forgiveness and new life are found through His death and resurrection.
For the parent who has already cut off an adult child solely because that child rejected Christianity, perhaps this article is stirring something painful.
You may have believed you were being faithful.
You may have been advised to do it.
You may have feared that maintaining contact would communicate approval.
But perhaps you now see that there is room to reconsider.
You do not have to settle every theological disagreement before making a phone call.
You do not have to promise to affirm everything your child believes.
You can begin with humility.

“I've been thinking about how we've handled things. I still love Jesus, and my convictions remain. But I regret making you feel that you had to share my beliefs to have a relationship with me. If you're willing, I would like us to talk.”
Your child may not respond.
They may need time.
They may have wounds you do not yet understand.
They may decline contact.
Respect that.
Reconciliation cannot be demanded.
And an apology is not a transaction that guarantees immediate access to another person's life.
But you can take responsibility for your part.
You can leave room for an honest response.
You can seek counsel from mature believers who understand Scripture and family relationships.
You can pray without using prayer as a substitute for the difficult work of listening.
And where abuse or serious danger exists, you can pursue wisdom and safety rather than rushing into unsafe contact.
This is not about making every family look perfect.
It is about becoming more faithful to Christ within the family you actually have.
And now I want to speak to the parent who is quietly crying while reading this.
The one who has prayed for years.
The one who still remembers their child's little voice singing worship songs.
The one who sees an empty seat at church and feels the ache all over again.
The one who wonders whether God hears the prayers whispered late at night.
I cannot promise you that your child will return to faith.
No faithful reading of Scripture gives me the right to guarantee the conversion of a particular person.
And I will not use your pain to offer a promise God has not made.
But I can remind you that God is worthy of trust even when the outcome remains uncertain.
He is not limited by your ability to persuade.
He is not confused by your child's questions.
He is not intimidated by unbelief.
And He does not need you to become harsh in order to defend His holiness.
Keep praying.
Keep speaking truth when there is an appropriate opportunity.
Keep living the gospel you proclaim.
Keep your boundaries wise.
Keep your conscience clear.
And when fear rises, remember that your child's eternal destiny does not rest upon your ability to control every conversation.
You are called to be faithful.
God remains God.
Maybe tonight, instead of composing another argument, you need to pray a different prayer.

“Father, I love my child, and I am afraid. Forgive me where fear has made me controlling. Forgive me where anger has made me unkind. Show me where I need to repent. Give me courage to stand for Your truth without using it as a weapon. Protect my child. Open doors for honest conversation. Draw them to Jesus according to Your mercy. And teach me to love faithfully even when I cannot control the outcome. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And perhaps the next step is not a sermon.
Perhaps it is a simple message.
“Thinking of you today. I love you. I hope you're doing well.”
No hidden argument.
No trap.
No condition attached.
Just an open door, where an open door is safe and appropriate.
Because sometimes a child who has stopped listening to your sermons is still watching your life.
They notice whether your faith makes you patient.
Whether your convictions make you humble.
Whether you apologize.
Whether you tell the truth.
Whether you love people who cannot give you what you want.
They are watching whether the Jesus you proclaim is reflected in the way you treat them.
And while your behavior cannot save anyone, your conduct can either support or undermine the credibility of your witness.
So here is the answer to the question that brought us here.
Should Christian parents cut off an adult child who rejects their faith?
Not simply because that child no longer believes.
The Bible does not command such a blanket cutoff.
There may be circumstances requiring firm boundaries, restricted contact, or separation because of abuse, danger, or persistent destructive behavior.
There may be painful disagreements that cannot be resolved.
There may be relationships where peace is not presently possible.
But unbelief alone is not a biblical command to withdraw parental love.
You can remain faithful to Jesus without making your child earn your affection through religious agreement.
You can refuse to compromise without refusing to care.
You can grieve without condemning every conversation to conflict.
You can hold the truth firmly while holding your own pride loosely.
And you can remember that the gospel is not the story of people who earned God's love by becoming acceptable first.
It is the story of Jesus Christ, who came to save sinners.
The cross does not minimize sin.
It reveals how serious sin is.
And it reveals how extraordinary God's mercy is.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about winning arguments or defending religious identity.
It is about Jesus.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who died for our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One in whom forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life are found.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because truth is negotiable.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
And that includes the way we respond when the people we love disappoint us.
If this article has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you are the parent who needs to apologize.
Maybe you are the adult child who needs healing.
Maybe you are still trying to understand how to love someone without compromising your faith.
Maybe you have been carrying a prayer request for so long that you no longer know how to put it into words.
And if you have a testimony of reconciliation, repentance, or renewed faith, consider sharing it. Someone else may need the encouragement that God has not finished working in human hearts.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.
That kind of work takes time, resources, and consistent support.
Not because you owe this ministry a payment for receiving the gospel.
But because voluntary generosity can be one practical way of helping gospel-centered resources reach more people.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which I want to invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
These items are not the reason the gospel matters.
They are simply practical resources and expressions of appreciation for those helping the ministry continue.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Make use of the free resources.
Your worth in Christ is not measured by what you can give to a ministry.
And the gospel must never become something available only to those who can afford it.
What matters is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully, Scripture is handled responsibly, and people are encouraged toward genuine repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformation through Him.
Before you leave, I want you to return to that road in Luke 15.
Picture the father again.
Looking into the distance.
The son who left has returned.
His clothes are worn.
His plans have collapsed.
His confession is beginning.
And the father runs.
The story does not tell us how long he waited.
It does not promise every wandering child will return.
It does not teach us to tolerate abuse or abandon boundaries.
But it does show us a father whose mercy is greater than his desire to humiliate a repentant son.
And it invites us to consider the mercy of God.
So, Christian parent, stand for Jesus.
Do not surrender the truth.
Do not pretend unbelief does not matter.
But do not confuse cruelty with courage.
Do not confuse silence used as punishment with holiness.
Do not confuse your ability to control a relationship with your ability to save a soul.
And if the road between you and your child has become painfully long, ask God for wisdom about what faithfulness looks like today.
Maybe it means a boundary.
Maybe it means an apology.
Maybe it means listening.
Maybe it means speaking truth gently.
Maybe it means allowing time.
And maybe, where it is safe and welcome, it means keeping a light on without demanding that your child pretend to believe before they can come home.
Because the child who no longer shares your faith should never have to wonder whether your love was real.
